newsitem.title: FRANCE: French capital markets closing report.
newsitem.headline: French capital markets closing report.

text.p: French bonds shrugged off strong U.S. economic data to climb to their highest level for a week but traders said the gains were fragile and there was a limit to how long European bonds could outperform the United States.

Traders said the market was driven up initially by traders covering short positions put on after Federal Reserve chairman Alan Greenspan's speech and then partly by market makers who had sold puts at 132. The March bond option expired today.
However, a spurt from the Bund market after the U.S. durable goods orders pushed French bonds up to 132.22, filling a gap left earlier this week.
Some traders said the strength in the German market came on hopes there would be an agreement next week on tax reforms between the Christian Democrats and the opposition Social Democrats.

Analysts said although French and German bonds have largely ignored the decline in U.S. bonds, the 10-year spreads had now widened to such a point where European bonds could be vulnerable to any further U.S. declines.
The spread between French and U.S. 10-year bonds widened to 127 basis points on Thursday compared with 100 basis points a week ago and 45 basis points six months ago.

"Our official view is we can go to 125 (basis points over German 10-year bonds) because Europe is in a mess from a growth perspective, putting back the possibility of rate rises, whereas in the States there's scope for higher long yields," Joanne Perez, strategist at Merrill Lynch said.

"It's difficult to see given the weakness of the mark why we should have spreads wider than that," she said. "If we get a real bear market performance in the U.S. the markets are sufficiently long in Europe to want to protect themselves."
Iain Lindsay at Credit Lyonnais said it would be hard to sell French and German bonds with such high spreads.
"If there's any further knock to Treasuries, European bonds are more likely to suffer," Lindsay said.
A trader said the bond future's gains looked to be limited at 132.50 and any losses would be supported at 131.50 ahead of key U.S. jobs statistics next week.
Lindsay said U.S. and German jobs data would be the most important factors for the bond market next week.

Analysts said PIBOR contracts with maturities in 1998 were suffering slightly from the perception that signs of better than expected growth in France had raised the chances of interest rate rises in the year to come.
"With such a flat PIBOR curve you can start pricing in a rate hike in 1998," Lindsay said.
As expected, the Bank of France left the intervention rate unchanged at 3.10 percent at a regular money market tender on Thursday. Both March and June PIBOR settled up one basis point at 96.64.
The franc slipped slightly against the mark to 3.3742 compared with 3.3721 on Wednesday.
Call money was unchanged at 3-1/8 1/4 percent.
